rubrics.evidence: The executive recommendation makes “A real venture experiment” the “central learning laboratory.” Phases 1–4 require customer interviews, pricing experiments, an MVP, pilots and financing scenarios; degrees are conditional on a separate decision rule.
rubrics.reason: Practical venture-building determines the roadmap and its progression, while another broad degree is explicitly deprioritized for someone with MBA-level knowledge.

rubrics.evidence: The plan begins at “5–7 hours per week,” provides a six-hour weekly schedule, and limits participation to “one primary course and one primary venture experiment at a time.” Accelerator participation requires “planned leave, a sabbatical or a properly financed transition.”
rubrics.reason: Work and family compatibility materially shapes scheduling, education branches and workload limits. Disruptive accelerators are reserved for validated ventures and an explicit change in employment commitment.

rubrics.evidence: Months 1–3 target “25–30 interviews” with “no product development beyond sketches or mock-ups.” Months 4–6 require a willingness-to-pay test, a manual-service offer or prototype, and pricing experiments, followed by a continuation gate: “If evidence is weak, pivot or stop.”
rubrics.reason: Low-cost discovery starts alongside initial education, and progressively stronger commercial tests precede MVP development and larger commitments. Explicit gates make validation consequential rather than merely aspirational.

rubrics.evidence: Non-degree selection criteria require “at least half the assessed work” to apply to the venture and mandatory customer experiments. Phase 2 requires competitor analysis, observed buying behavior, top-down and bottom-up market sizing, unit economics and an assumptions register. Online learning must produce “a customer-facing action, a decision, or a reusable venture artifact.”
rubrics.reason: Resource selection and assignments emphasize concrete frameworks, market evidence and application to actual venture decisions rather than passive theoretical study.

rubrics.evidence: The comparison includes tuition, weekly commitments, dilution and opportunity costs. The degree decision rule considers employer sponsorship and venture-for-credit opportunities; executive education is assessed by whether it creates relationships or decisions unavailable through “six weeks of independent work.” Accelerators are treated as “financing and company-building decisions, not inexpensive education.”
rubrics.reason: Cost, time and incremental practical value directly determine when each route is justified. The default remains targeted education and venture experiments, with expensive or disruptive options conditional on specific benefits.
